name: Public binding free energy benchmark (Ross et al. 2023)
description: Assembled collection of proteins and congeneric small-molecule series with measured affinities, used to score relative binding free energy predictions against experiment.

attributes.version: As curated for Ross et al. 2023; data released as the public_binding_free_energy_benchmark repository, releases v1.0 and v2.0 (both 2023-06-26, MIT)
attributes.task: Relative binding affinity prediction for congeneric series
attributes.scope_note: Table 3 (FEP+ accuracy beside experimental reproducibility), Table 2 (the data sets and their compound counts) and Table 1 (the assay-reproducibility survey) extracted. Per-system values in the Supplementary Results and the repository were not retrieved. The Boltz-2 supplement's two subsets of this collection are recorded as separate protocols.
attributes.source_locator: Ross et al. 2023 Tables 1-3; Boltz-2 supplement appendix D.2.1 and E.2.1
limitations: Ross et al. 2023 states its results use release v1.0 of the public benchmark repository; the Boltz-2 supplement does not state which release its subsets come from.

The 876-complex OpenFE subset and the 87-compound 4-target subset both derive from this collection and must partly overlap, so results on the two subsets are not independent. Neither source states the overlap.

name: FEP+ protocol tuned per system after seeing the error against experiment
description: Limit the Boltz-2 supplement states about the FEP+ arm it compares against.

attributes.value: The Boltz-2 supplement states that 'The results of FEP+ are intended to show the maximum attainable accuracy of current (commercial) FEP simulations by manually adjusting the protocol (input preparation, perturbation map, force field) to the system at hand after observing the error with respect to the experiment [Ross et al., 2023]'. Tables 11, 12 and 14 print one value per cell with no uncertainty. Bootstrap standard errors appear only as error bars in Figure 6, which prints no numbers.

The results of FEP+ are intended to show the maximum attainable accuracy of current (commercial) FEP simulations by manually adjusting the protocol (input preparation, perturbation map, force field) to the system at hand after observing the error with respect to the experiment (appendix D.2.2, 'Baselines'), so the FEP+ arm is not a prospective baseline.
The ABFE arm 'may also represent an optimistic estimate of its prospective performance given that the protocol was optimized based this dataset' (appendix D.2.2, 'Baselines').
The OpenFE arm's cited source is a blog post (Horton, 2025), which is not a primary source under this repository's rules and was not retrieved.

The column headers read 'target avg.' while appendix D.2.2 'Evaluation metrics' defines every regression metric as computed per assay and averaged across assays weighted by compound count. Assays and targets are not the same unit, and the source does not reconcile the two labels.
The paper's claim of being more than 1,000 times faster than FEP is not backed by a measured FEP+ cost: the FEP+ time cell in Table 12 is printed as '-'.
Per-assay and per-series values behind the target averages are not printed anywhere in the supplement. Figure 12 shows per-assay scatter plots for the validation set only and prints no numbers.

description: Which method ranks a hit's close analogues by binding affinity accurately enough to choose what to make next, and at what compute cost against free energy calculation?

attributes.question: Which method ranks a hit's close analogues by binding affinity accurately enough to choose what to make next, and at what compute cost against free energy calculation?
intended_users: Medicinal chemists choosing which analogues of a confirmed hit to synthesise next
Computational chemists deciding whether to spend free energy calculation on a series
Project leads budgeting compute against synthesis in a lead-optimisation campaign
attributes.decision: Choose which analogues of a confirmed hit to make next, and choose the method and compute budget used to rank them.
inputs: A confirmed hit and a set of close analogues, with the series' chemical relationship stated
A protein structure or sequence for the target, and its relationship to any structure used in training
Measured affinities for part of the series, with the assay type and units recorded
An available compute budget and a synthesis budget
attributes.output: A ranking of the analogues by predicted binding affinity, with an error estimate against measured affinities on comparable series, the leakage control that estimate rests on, and the compute cost of producing it.
attributes.setting: Research-stage lead optimisation within one target's congeneric series. Ranking across unrelated targets, hit discovery from a large library and absolute affinity prediction are separate questions.
exclusions: No reviewed source in this batch publishes a per-series affinity-ranking value for any method: every extracted number is an average across series, so none of them says how well a given series would be ranked.
A correlation pooled or averaged over unrelated targets does not answer this question and flatters every method.
Accuracy on a benchmark series does not establish that a chosen analogue will be more potent, nor that it will be developable.
IC50, Ki and Kd are not interchangeable; sources that convert between them do so under a stated assumption that must be carried with the number.
Compute-cost comparisons are only meaningful against a measured alternative. The extracted tables print no measured cost for FEP+.
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Affinity ranking does not establish efficacy, safety or clinical suitability.
evidence_gaps: Automated source review only; independent human scientific review remains outstanding.

No per-series value is published for any method in the extracted sources. The route to per-series evidence is the public_binding_free_energy_benchmark repository (MIT, releases v1.0 and v2.0), which holds FEP+ per-edge results, and the OpenFE per-transformation deposits on Zenodo; nothing was computed from either in this pass.

No fully independent evaluation of a machine-learning affinity predictor against free energy calculation on the same measured congeneric series was found. Both same-series comparisons that exist are reported by the developers of the machine-learning method, and both take their FEP+ arm from a benchmark whose protocol was tuned per system after seeing the error against experiment.

The peer-reviewed OpenFE industry benchmark (doi 10.1021/acs.jcim.6c00089) is behind an ACS paywall and was not retrieved, so the open-source free energy arm rests on a blog post the Boltz-2 supplement cites.
No measured compute cost for FEP+ exists in any extracted table; the only cost column prints '-' for FEP+ and ranges for OpenFE and ABFE.
No uncertainty is printed for any Boltz-2 supplement cell; the bootstrap error bars are figure-only.
The CASP16 assessors' per-group and per-target Kendall tau values are figure-only and were not extracted; the official per-target results file was not downloaded.

Neither the Merck FEP benchmark (Schindler et al. 2020) nor the Hahn et al. 2022 benchmark-construction paper nor the Wu et al. 2025 ABFE protocol paper was retrieved, so the series definitions behind the four-target subset are not established.

MM/GBSA and docking-score comparators on congeneric series were not searched for beyond the arms the Boltz-2 supplement chose for itself; recent affinity models other than Boltz-2, GAT and BACPI were not covered.
The overlap between the 876-complex OpenFE subset and the 87-compound four-target subset is not stated in any source, so the two comparisons cannot be treated as independent.

attributes.value:
Three sources carry the extracted evidence, and none of them publishes a per-series value: every number below is an average across congeneric series.

Ross et al. 2023, written by the developers of the FEP+ workflow, sets both the free energy baseline and the assay noise floor on the same page. On a curated collection of 1,237 compounds across more than 50 proteins, FEP+ reached a compound-weighted pairwise RMSE of 1.25 kcal/mol [1.17, 1.33], a pairwise mean unsigned error of 0.98 [0.91, 1.05], a coefficient of determination of 0.56 [0.51, 0.60] and a Kendall tau of 0.51 [0.48, 0.55]; its edgewise errors, which depend on the perturbation graph's topology, were 1.17 [1.08, 1.25] and 0.91 [0.84, 0.98]. The same table's survey of 1,867 compounds whose affinities were measured in at least two independent assays gives the noise floor: pairwise RMSE 0.91 kcal/mol [0.83, 1.11], mean unsigned error 0.67 [0.61, 0.83], R2 0.79 [0.75, 0.82] and Kendall tau 0.71 [0.65, 0.74]. So the error of the free energy calculation is close to the error between two assays, while its rank correlation sits well below. The FEP+ protocol was adjusted by hand per system after the error against experiment had been seen, so this is a maximum-attainable rather than a prospective figure.

The Boltz-2 supplement, written by the developers of Boltz-2, is the only source here that puts a machine-learning predictor beside free energy calculation on the same compounds. On 876 protein-ligand complexes from the same collection, Boltz-2 reached an assay-weighted Pearson R of 0.62 and Kendall tau of 0.46, against 0.63 and 0.47 for OpenFE under a fixed automated protocol and 0.72 and 0.53 for FEP+; the sequence-only baselines reached 0.29 and 0.19 (BACPI) and 0.28 and 0.20 for its ligand-only ablation, and Boltz-2's own interface confidence score reached -0.07 and -0.05. On a four-target subset of 87 neutral compounds the supplement prints compute cost beside accuracy: Boltz-2 0.66 and 0.48 at 20 GPU seconds, OpenFE 0.66 and 0.51 at 6-12 GPU hours, ABFE 0.75 and 0.54 at more than 20 GPU hours, FEP+ 0.78 and 0.63 with its time cell printed as '-', FMO 0.55 and 0.38 at 2-10 CPU minutes, Chemgauss4 0.26 and 0.17 at 20-30 CPU seconds and MM/PBSA 0.18 and 0.16 at 10-15 CPU minutes. No measured FEP+ cost appears in the table. On the CASP16 blind challenge, where the mmseqs 90% identity filtering used for the other benchmarks was not applied because the data postdates the training cutoff, the supplement reports Boltz-2 at 0.65 and 0.45 against the highest-ranked participant at 0.54 and 0.42. Tables 11, 12 and 14 print one value per cell with no uncertainty.

The independent CASP16 assessment sets those challenge figures against a ceiling. Its abstract gives the maximum Kendall tau across all participants as 0.42, against an estimated best achievable value of 0.73 derived by resampling the measurements under an assumed threefold IC50 error (0.54 with a standard deviation of 0.11 for chymase, 0.76 with 0.02 for autotaxin); under an assumed 30-fold error the expected best tau for autotaxin falls to 0.43. Its body text gives the maximum achieved value as 0.39 for one figure and 'about 0.4' elsewhere without reconciling the three numbers, and it scores submissions under its own weighting and skip conventions, so its 0.42 and the 0.42 printed for group LG016 in the Boltz-2 supplement are not established to be the same quantity. Supplying experimental structures in stage 2 produced no shift toward greater accuracy, and the assessors note that the best CASP16 stage-1 results are no better than the typical best stage 1 D3R result, which averaged a Kendall tau of 0.48 with a minimum of 0.21 and a maximum of 0.71.

Two comparisons bear on the use case's question and both are author-reported: the Boltz-2 supplement's two FEP+ benchmark subsets. Both take their FEP+ arm from a benchmark whose protocol was tuned per system after seeing the experimental error, and both average over series rather than printing per-series values, so neither can say how well a given series would be ranked.
